# Declaring done before you start: goals as a yardstick
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/blog/declaring-done-before-you-start
Description: Decide what finished looks like before your first prompt. What Scrum and vendor docs say about done, and how to write a yardstick an agent can check.

There's a moment at the start of most sessions when you know what you want and haven't said what "finished" looks like. You type the request and send it. The agent starts. Somewhere later it stops, and you find yourself deciding, on the spot and a bit tired, whether this is done. We've done it more times than we'd like to admit.

## Done is easier to define before the work

Software teams have a name for this. The Scrum Guide asks teams for a Definition of Done, which it describes as a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product.1 The idea is plain. A team agrees what counts as finished first, so finishing isn't a mood.

A solo builder with an agent doesn't have a team to agree with. That makes it easier to skip, and it's why we think it's worth doing on purpose. The agreement is just between you and the task.

## What a vendor says about "looks done"

Anthropic's best practices guide for Claude Code is a vendor document, so it speaks for that tool only, and we're citing it for what it says rather than for anything about how a model works. On stopping, it says that Claude stops when the work looks done, and that without a check it can run, "looks done" is the only signal available, which makes you the verification loop.2

That sentence describes the problem from the agent's side, and it maps neatly onto the human side too. If you haven't said what done means, "looks done" is the only signal you have either.

The same guide gives a concrete contrast. Its example of a better prompt isn't "implement a function that validates email addresses". It's a validateEmail function with example test cases, and an instruction to run the tests after implementing.2 The second version contains its own yardstick. Anyone can read the output and say whether it passed.

## What a good yardstick holds

Claude Code's documentation for its /goal command is the clearest written description we've found of a completion condition. It says a condition that holds up across many turns usually has one measurable end state, a stated check, and constraints that matter.3 Its examples of an end state are a test result, a build exit code, a file count and an empty queue.

You don't need that command to borrow the shape. It works in any prompt, with any tool, or none:

- An end state you could observe. Not "cleaner", but "the test suite passes and the lint step is clean".

- A way to prove it. Which command, which screenshot, which output you expect to see.

- A fence. What must not change on the way there.

The goal documentation adds a detail we like. With /goal, completion is decided by a fresh model rather than the one doing the work.3 Whatever tool you use, the principle travels: the thing that did the work shouldn't be the only judge of it.

## When the yardstick is wrong

We should be honest about a limit. A yardstick written before the work is a guess, and sometimes the guess is wrong. Halfway through, you learn the real problem is somewhere else, and "all tests pass" no longer measures what you care about.

That isn't a failure of the habit. Changing the yardstick on purpose, and noticing that you did, is very different from drifting to a new one without saying so. The first is a decision. The second is how a build ends up somewhere nobody chose.

The same guide is blunt about shipping: if you can't verify it, don't ship it.2 We'd add a gentler version for the start of a session. If you can't say how you'd verify it, you may not have finished deciding what you want.

## Reading the record afterwards

Cartographer reads the session history your coding agent already keeps and turns it into a map of how a project was built. When you mark a version shipped, partial or abandoned and say what actually happened, it appraises each session's moves against the outcome you declared. A yardstick written down early gives that comparison something firm to measure against. It reads what's already on your machine, with no cloud.

## A small habit

Before your next first prompt, write one more sentence. Say what you'd see if this went well, and how you'd check. Put it in the prompt, or keep it in a note. Then, when the agent stops, you're comparing against something you wrote when you were fresh, not something you invented when you were tired.

## Sources

- Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland. The Scrum Guide. scrumguides.org, 2020.

- Anthropic. Best practices for Claude Code. Claude Code documentation, code.claude.com.

- Anthropic. Keep Claude working toward a goal. Claude Code documentation, code.claude.com.

Questions, or a topic you'd like us to dig into next? Reach out any time: support@codecartographer.dev. We read everything.

# Why a correction is the most informative prompt in a session
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/blog/why-a-correction-is-the-most-informative-prompt
Description: A correction tells you what you meant, what the agent assumed, and where they split. Here's what research and vendor docs say, and how to read yours.

Scroll back through a long session and most of it blurs. Requests, replies, more requests. Then you hit one of your own messages that begins "No, not that" or "I meant the other file", and it stops you. Something happened there. We'd argue it's the most informative line in the whole transcript.

## What a correction carries

An ordinary prompt is a hope. It describes an outcome you haven't seen yet. A correction is different, because it's a judgment made against something real. You looked at what came back, compared it with what you meant, and found a gap. Then you wrote the gap down.

So a single correction holds three things at once. It holds what you meant, which was often fuzzier in your head than in your first prompt. It holds what the agent took you to mean. And it holds the exact place where the two split. Few other lines in a session do that much work in so few words.

To be clear, that's our reading, not a finding. No study we know of measures "information in a correction." What the research does show is narrower, and it points the same way.

## What the research says about fixing errors

Suzhen Zhong, Ying Zou and Bram Adams studied real conversations between developers and a large language model, building a dataset called CodeChat from them. Among their findings: prompts that point out mistakes in code generated in prior turns and explicitly request a fix are most effective for resolving errors.1

Read that closely. The effective move isn't a louder "try again." It names the mistake and asks for the fix. That's a correction doing its job: it carries the gap along with it, so the next attempt has something to aim at.

The same paper reports that syntax and import errors persist across turns of a conversation.1 Problems don't always melt away on their own. Somebody has to notice them and say so, and that somebody is usually you.

## What the vendor docs say about timing

Anthropic's best practices guide for Claude Code is a vendor document, so it speaks only for that tool. We cite it for what it says, not for anything about how any model works inside. The guide advises that you correct Claude as soon as you notice it going off track, and says the best results come from tight feedback loops.2

It also names a failure pattern worth knowing. The guide says that if you've corrected Claude more than twice on the same issue in one session, the context is cluttered with failed approaches, and it suggests clearing and starting again with a more specific prompt that uses what you learned.2

Put the two together and a correction has a second job. Besides steering the next reply, it tells you something about your own prompt. One correction is normal. Three on the same point is a sign the original ask was missing something, and the pile of corrections is the evidence of what.

## Reading your corrections afterwards

Here's a small exercise. After a session, skip everything else and read only your corrections, in order. A few patterns tend to show up.

- The same correction twice. Something you assumed was obvious never made it into a prompt or a project note.

- A correction that changes direction. Your goal moved, and the first prompt no longer describes it.

- A correction that narrows scope. You were clear about what to do, and less clear about what to leave alone.

- A correction you almost didn't make. Those are the ones to be honest about, because they mark where you nearly accepted something you didn't understand.

None of these labels come from a study. They're what we notice when we reread our own sessions. Your list may look different, and that's fine. The point is that corrections are already sorted for you: they're the moments you disagreed.

That's where a session record earns its keep. Cartographer reads the session history your coding agent already keeps and turns it into a map of how a project was built. Each move on the map records what you did: the prompt, the correction, the decision, the pause. Dead ends and fixes get marked, so the places where you steered are easy to find. It reads what's already on your machine, with no cloud.

## A habit worth keeping

Next time you type "no, I meant", pause for a second and finish the thought. What did you mean? What did the agent assume instead? If you can say both in a sentence, put that sentence in the correction. The research suggests naming the mistake helps, and it'll help you later when you read the record back.

A correction can feel like friction, a small tax on getting things done. We'd rather think of it as the session telling you the truth about itself.

## Sources

- Suzhen Zhong, Ying Zou and Bram Adams. Developer-LLM Conversations: An Empirical Study of Interactions and Generated Code Quality. arXiv:2509.10402, 2025.

- Anthropic. Best practices for Claude Code. Claude Code documentation, code.claude.com.

Questions, or a topic you'd like us to dig into next? Reach out any time: mapit@codecartographer.dev. We read everything.

# What the research says about reviewing code you didn't write
URL: https://codecartographer.dev/blog/reviewing-code-you-did-not-write
Description: Two studies of code review put understanding the change first. Here's what they found, and what it means when you didn't write the code.

Most of us picture code review as hunting. You scan a diff, you spot the off-by-one, you flag it. The research paints a different picture, and it's worth knowing before you sit down to read the next change you didn't write.

## Review isn't mostly about bugs

In 2013, Alberto Bacchelli and Christian Bird studied code review at Microsoft. They observed, interviewed and surveyed developers and managers, and they classified hundreds of review comments across diverse teams. Their finding was that finding defects remains the main motivation for review, but reviews are less about defects than expected.1 People got other things out of it too: knowledge transfer, team awareness, and alternative solutions to the problem at hand.1

The part that matters most for us is what they named as the center of the activity. In their words, code and change understanding is the key aspect of code reviewing, and developers used mechanisms to get it that current tools don't meet.1

## What reviewers actually do

A more recent study looks at the how. Pavlína Wurzel Gonçalves and colleagues, writing for the 2025 International Conference on Program Comprehension, observed and interviewed ten experienced reviewers as they worked through 25 reviews, and read what they saw through code comprehension theory.2

They report that reviewers work opportunistically. The strategies they describe usually start with a phase of building context. Only then does the reviewer move into inspecting the code, which involves reading it, testing it, and managing discussion.2

Notice the order. Context comes first, and reading the lines comes second.

## What this means when you didn't write it

Neither study was about coding agents, and we won't pretend otherwise. They looked at people reviewing changes made by other people. What follows is our own reading, not a finding.

If understanding is the hard part of review, then the least understood changes are the riskiest ones to wave through. A change you didn't write, made for reasons you weren't in the room for, starts you at zero. That's true of a colleague's pull request. We'd argue it's just as true of code that arrived while you were typing prompts and watching a terminal scroll.

So the studies suggest a few habits that cost very little:

- Build context before you read the diff. What was this change meant to do, and why now?

- Treat "I can't explain this yet" as a real review result, not a delay.

- Test it, don't just read it. Testing is part of how experienced reviewers inspect code in the second study.

- Keep notes on the reasons behind the change, so you aren't rebuilding them from memory later.

That last one is where a session record helps. Cartographer reads the session history your coding agent already keeps and turns it into a map of how a project was built: what you asked, what happened, and how you responded. It reads what's already on your machine, with no cloud. When you come back to a change weeks later, the context you'd have to rebuild is already written down.

## Why this is a kindness to your future self

There's a quieter point here. Understanding is work, and work gets skipped when we're tired or when a change looks tidy. A clean diff feels like a finished thought. It isn't evidence that anyone understood it, least of all you.

We've all approved something because the tests passed and the summary sounded sure of itself. Sometimes that's fine. But passing tests tell you the code does what the tests ask, not that you know what you've agreed to carry. When something breaks months later, the person who has to untangle it is you, and you'll be reading it cold.

None of this needs a new tool or a long checklist. It needs a pause long enough to say, in your own words, what the change does and why it exists. If you can't, you've learned something useful, and it cost you a minute instead of a week.

## A small shift in the question

"Is this correct?" is a fine question. But the research suggests it comes second. First comes "do I understand what this change is trying to do?" If the answer is no, the review hasn't really started, and that's worth knowing before you hit merge.

## Sources

- Alberto Bacchelli and Christian Bird. Expectations, Outcomes, and Challenges of Modern Code Review. 35th International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE), 2013.

- Pavlína Wurzel Gonçalves, Pooja Rani, Margaret-Anne Storey, Diomidis Spinellis and Alberto Bacchelli. Code Review Comprehension: Reviewing Strategies Seen Through Code Comprehension Theories. International Conference on Program Comprehension (ICPC), 2025. arXiv:2503.21455.

Questions, or a topic you'd like us to dig into next? Reach out any time: support@codecartographer.dev. We read everything.
